video_title: USV’s New $900M Fund: Fred Wilson, Rebecca Kaden & Mike Mignano
gist: USV partners Fred Wilson, Rebecca Kaden and Mike Mignano discuss closing a $900M fund (largest ever, ~30-40 companies, larger Series A checks of $10-30M, more seeds and incubations) and a thesis built on AI application-layer 'obliterate, don't automate', open-source 'Rebel Alliance' infrastructure and energy. Includes an office tour and a hot take that user interfaces will survive agents.

themes.theme: USV $900M fund: size, strategy and check construction

insights.claim: Union Square Ventures raised $900M in new funds, by far its largest cycle, framed as a bottoms-up strategy number (roughly 30-40 companies, more seeds) rather than a vanity milestone; the explicit reason is that rounds are bigger, faster and more expensive and outcomes/swings are larger.
insights.speaker: Mike Mignano
insights.so_what: Even a thesis-driven small early-stage fund is scaling up to hold ownership targets as AI-era round sizes inflate.

insights.claim: USV keeps its Series A focus but writes larger checks (10-30M in Series A, rounds can be larger) purely to hit ownership targets and fund math as round sizes inflate; a typical Series A 'starts with 10' million now, with some A rounds at 100M or even a billion.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Series A price discovery has moved an order of magnitude from the ~$3M A check USV started with; small funds must grow checks just to hold ownership.

insights.claim: Seed strategy is shifting toward proprietary deal formation: pure founder bets, incubations, and partnering with an entrepreneur on an idea with USV supplying the first two checks; these could be a third to a half of all seed investments.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Signals the seed market is so competitive that top thesis funds manufacture their own deal flow rather than compete for allocations.

insights.claim: USV argues small fund size aligns incentives (easier to return the fund and reach carry, pickier, results focused on portfolio performance) and that LPs, to Rebecca Kaden's surprise, asked 'are you sure you shouldn't raise more?' because they see the same market shifts.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Kaden
insights.so_what: LP appetite for larger sizing from disciplined small managers suggests capital is chasing venture access and fund-size restraint is being re-priced.

insights.claim: USV does not need to underwrite trillion-dollar outcomes: with its fund size and ownership, winners in the single-digit billions produce healthy returns, most of its biggest winners are around $10B, and only a few are outliers at $50B-$100B.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Return math for a $900M early-stage fund is built on $5-10B exits, which makes mid-size M&A and secondary buyers relevant exits.
insights.quote: I don't think a trillion is what we need to underwrite to at USV.

insights.claim: USV believes value is aggregating to the top one or two players in a market faster than ever and the long tail is not getting interest, so it is less willing to underwrite a number three or four player as it might have in earlier eras.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Kaden
insights.so_what: Winner-take-most dynamics in AI-era categories push early-stage investors to concentrate on category leaders and pay up for them.

insights.claim: USV deliberately underwrites markets that barely exist yet (crypto at the Coinbase investment, energy/nuclear via Radiant, robotics via sensor proliferation) and treats every investment as a TAM-expansion bet rather than a fixed-TAM model.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Kaden
insights.so_what: Thesis-driven forward underwriting, not current spend, is how USV claims to find outlier returns.

themes.theme: AI application layer, consumer agents and who needs capital

insights.claim: USV frames today as analogous to 2003: AI infrastructure is largely built (like Google, Amazon, Yahoo, eBay then) while the big applications (the Facebook/Twitter/YouTube/iPhone equivalents) are still to come, and it sees the start of an application-layer explosion driven by agents.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Positions the investable window for AI as application-layer rather than infrastructure, with historical precedent of the 2003-2007 cohort.

insights.claim: Startups are increasingly subsidizing inference for customers to reach adoption, and OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini still subsidize core chat for free, so building large-scale consumer AI businesses is capital intensive; this is a reason round sizes are rising even as building a product gets cheaper.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Kaden
insights.so_what: Compute subsidy is the new CAC; consumer AI winners need balance sheets, which favors well-funded or distribution-advantaged players.

insights.claim: Capital use has shifted from building the product to breaking through the noise: with building easier than ever, much of the money goes to marketing, messaging, positioning and go-to-market, especially in consumer.
insights.speaker: Mike Mignano
insights.so_what: Distribution and narrative, not engineering, are the scarce inputs, shifting where venture dollars go.

insights.claim: USV sees two possible consumer-agent paths: win by scale and distribution, or (its Twitter-era view) still need network effects by turning single-player agent behavior into multiplayer; it has not yet seen the multiplayer breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Kaden
insights.so_what: A live open question for agent-app moats; whoever cracks multiplayer agents may have durable retention that scale-only players lack.

insights.claim: Fred Wilson expects people to want a personal agent that talks to Amazon's, Etsy's and Shopify's agents instead of agents logging in as the user; Amazon is already blocking third-party agents (reportedly telling Facebook it would not let its agent access Amazon), so standards for agent-to-agent connection will emerge.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Platform gatekeepers blocking agent access sets up a protocol/standards fight and an opening for agent-interoperability infrastructure.

insights.claim: Contrarian view that the user interface is not dying: agents will handle shopping and taxes, but people will still want to watch Netflix, YouTube and scroll feeds themselves, and UI is where users build trust, so everything collapsing into a chatbot is unlikely.
insights.speaker: Mike Mignano
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the chatbot-everywhere thesis; consumer products with strong interfaces and entertainment use keep value.
insights.quote: the user interface is not going away

insights.claim: Consumer AI trial behavior is at an all-time high while engagement is at a low, so paid trials and annual subscriptions inflate ARR without proving product love; USV looks past ARR to true usage retention (daily/weekly return, month-one churn) and cohort data matched with personal product use.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Kaden
insights.so_what: ARR in AI consumer apps is a weak signal; diligence should focus on usage cohorts, a likely source of overvaluation in recent rounds.
insights.quote: trial behavior is at an absolute high

themes.theme: Obliterate, don't automate: AI restructuring of markets

insights.claim: USV's application thesis 'obliterate, don't automate' (Fred's 2014 blog post) holds that AI lets consumers and businesses bypass gatekept professional services (lawyers, accountants, doctors, financial managers) rather than make incumbents more efficient, restructuring whole markets and moving value to the end user.
insights.speaker: Mike Mignano
insights.so_what: Highest-conviction application bet: AI-native replacement of service professions, not AI sold to those professionals.

insights.claim: Fred says 20 to 30% of USV's legal work no longer touches a human lawyer, including term sheets generated by a model trained on its own prior term sheets, and the share is rising.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Concrete early evidence of legal-work substitution inside a VC firm, pointing to pressure on legal-services economics.
insights.quote: 20 to 30% of the legal work that we do here at USV does not get touched by a human lawyer anymore.

insights.claim: Doctronic, a USV portfolio company, offers an AI doctor that can write prescriptions in some states (Utah currently, not controlled substances), which USV cites as the template for market-obliterating healthcare.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Regulatory permission for AI prescribing in a state is a leading indicator for AI-native healthcare access.

insights.claim: Incumbents in people-based businesses cannot adopt these models because doing so cannibalizes their payroll and billing model, and public incumbents answer to quarterly revenue; Brad Burnham's rule is the best time to bet against an incumbent is when doing what customers want threatens their current business, with Google cannibalizing search with Gemini as a counter-example only possible because of its other businesses.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Supports disruptor-over-incumbent positioning in services; Google is an exception because YouTube, Waymo, Gmail and Android subsidize search cannibalization.

insights.claim: USV's open question is not why incumbents can't do it but why anyone can't, since building is cheaper and faster, so advantage must come from network effects, speed, team, product decisions, and categories like physical AI, edge data and energy that behave unlike software.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Kaden
insights.so_what: Defensibility in AI apps is unresolved; this favors hard-to-replicate physical and network-effect businesses.

themes.theme: Rebel Alliance: open-source stack, energy and security

insights.claim: USV's 'Rebel Alliance' thesis is that developers fear building on closed frontier stacks (as with Facebook platform businesses that got cut out) and will assemble open-weight models, open harnesses, memory, routing and alignment layers; USV says few other VCs share its conviction here.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: An under-owned VC theme: open-source agent infrastructure layers could be bid up later if enterprises keep de-risking from closed labs.

insights.claim: Coinbase's CTO said at USV's CEO summit that Coinbase moved off Claude to its own coding-agent harness built on the open-source Pi project, from USV portfolio company Arendelle (as named in the transcript); Fred notes Shopify has done similar.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Public examples of large engineering orgs reducing dependency on a single frontier lab, a risk for lab enterprise revenue.

insights.claim: Fred pitches energy as the simple, levered way to bet on AI; energy (including micronuclear via Radiant, backed in 2021) is 20-30% of USV's portfolio, and USV sees cheaper programmable energy as the horizontal undercurrent beneath AI.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Shows a mainstream early-stage firm already concentrated in AI-adjacent energy; a read-through for private nuclear and power demand.

insights.claim: Consumer agent security is an emerging category: handing an agent email access breaks password-reset flows, so USV expects change in consumer cyber, on-device and private models, biometrics for proof of humanity, and has a portfolio sandbox company (Common Fabric) targeting this.
insights.speaker: Mike Mignano
insights.so_what: A new attack surface and a possible product gap in consumer agent security, with privacy-first products possibly getting a market they lacked before.

insights.claim: Trusted brands will matter in AI as they did in crypto: Coinbase built the most trusted brand in a sketchy industry by abstracting custody (cold storage, delayed withdrawals, two-factor) and Fred himself has been hacked four times in 15 years of owning crypto while keeping about 99% of holdings.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Trust and custody are the product in new asset or agent categories; AI companies telling people they will lose their jobs erodes that trust.

themes.theme: What makes winners: founders, non-linear paths and long holds

insights.claim: Winners are rarely straight lines: Abridge (transcribed as 'a bridge'; a 2016 USV company) first pursued a consumer go-to-market of patients recording doctor visits, only later finding doctors wanted the recording, and has made nearly all revenue for 5-6 years on one product before launching two more in the last 12 months.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: USV underwrites team and direction rather than the initial product, and expects pivots; patient capital matters for such outcomes.

insights.claim: USV's venture history shows roughly 2-3 outsized companies per early-stage fund across 10+ funds (Twitter, Etsy, Indeed in fund one; MongoDB, Twilio, Stripe, Coinbase, Duolingo later), and Fred suspects Indeed is 50-100x bigger than when USV sold.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Venture return is concentrated in 2-4 companies per fund, which is why USV holds for a decade and underwrites for outliers.

insights.claim: Team matters more than ever in this market because of intense talent competition from labs and incumbents paying a lot, narratives aggregating faster (the market designates winners well before the business exists), and the need for founders who can drive a story and go the distance.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Kaden
insights.so_what: Founder narrative skill is now an explicit investment criterion, which advantages storytellers and may inflate valuations ahead of fundamentals.
insights.quote: narratives and market narratives are aggregating faster than they ever have

insights.claim: USV admits it gets founder assessment wrong more than right: the failure modes are founders who overthink, struggle to recruit and retain, micromanage, or are slow to burn the boats and change a failing go-to-market.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Honest base rate on founder selection; informs diligence checklists for early-stage investing.

insights.claim: Early USV was in the camp arguing for free-to-users network building at Twitter and Facebook (Twitter's financing went from $5M to $25M to $100M in successive years) versus other VCs who wanted subscriptions; Fred says the same 10x scaling applies to today's rounds.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Historical analog for subsidized-growth AI products and the round-size inflation they require.

insights.claim: Large lab and open-source dynamics create unknown asymptotes: Rebecca notes compute is now a fundamental cost block, that how far compute costs fall and when models stall are unknown, and that startups like Instinct are projecting very large compute spend.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Kaden
insights.so_what: Compute cost trajectory is the swing factor for application-layer gross margins and thus for the AI venture thesis.

insights.claim: Late-stage valuation excess is expected and absorbed by buyers like Bending Spoons: companies valued at $5-10B that are worth about $1B will come back to earth, which suits acquirers that buy after the venture journey ends and re-run them under a different capital structure.
insights.speaker: Fred Wilson
insights.so_what: Supports a durable exit channel for down-valued unicorns at around $1B.
